Well, doctor, thank you for seeing me. It’s... gosh, it’s not easy for me to be sitting in this chair. You know, at my age—I’m 78 years old, I’ve lived a long life, I should have some sense of order and discipline by now. But instead, I’m dealing with this... this really distressing situation. I suppose it’s about my eating, but it’s more than just eating, it's... well, let me try to explain how it happens. 

It usually starts so innocently. I’ll be in the kitchen, maybe just meaning to have a small bite of something, just a cracker or a piece of bread. But then... and this is the part that really brings me in today, the part that honestly scares me most... once I start eating, it’s like I completely lose the steering wheel. It feels like my hands just take on a life of their own. They just keep reaching for more, opening the cupboards, pulling out boxes, just reaching and reaching. And the whole time, the entire time my hands are moving and I'm putting food in my mouth, I’m standing there in my own head literally telling myself, "Tom, stop this right now. You have to stop, Tom." 

But it doesn't matter what I say to myself. The hands just keep going, and I can't seem to make it stop no matter how hard I try to reason with myself. It's like I'm a passenger in my own body, just watching it happen...

No, no control at all. That’s exactly it, doctor. That’s the crux of the whole miserable thing. It’s... well, like I was just saying, it’s the most frightening part of all this. I mean, I’m an old man, I’ve worked hard my whole life, raised a family, paid my taxes, I’ve always prided myself on being a sensible person. But when this happens... when I take that first bite, whatever control I thought I had just vanishes into thin air. 

I’ll be standing right there in the middle of my kitchen—the same kitchen where my late wife used to bake her pies, God rest her soul—and my hands just take over. They just keep reaching and reaching, grabbing whatever is there. Cookies, bread, leftover casserole, it doesn't even matter what it is sometimes. And the whole time, the entire time, my mind is completely clear. I’m standing there, fully aware of what’s happening, and I’m literally screaming at myself in my head, "Tom, stop this right now! What on earth are you doing? You have to stop!" 

But the hands don't listen. It’s like there’s a disconnect between my brain and my body. I can see myself doing it, I can feel how full and sick I’m getting, but I just cannot force myself to stop until... well, until I’m completely stuffed and there's nothing left in front of me. It’s a terrible, helpless feeling, doctor. Just terrible. To be trapped inside yourself like that, unable to hit the brakes.

Guilty? Ashamed? Oh, doctor... you have no idea. The guilt is... it's heavy. It's like a physical weight sitting right on my chest. As soon as it's over, as soon as the frenzy stops and I'm just standing there looking at the empty wrappers and the crumbs all over the counter... the shame just washes over me like a cold bucket of water.

I'll spend the rest of the day just sitting in my recliner, staring at the television but not really watching it, just beating myself up over and over again. "Why did you do that, Tom? Pleasure? Enjoyment? Good heavens, no. No, doctor, there is absolutely no joy in it whatsoever. You'd think there would be, wouldn't you? I mean, eating is supposed to be one of life's simple pleasures, especially at my age when you don't have too many vices left. 

I remember when Mary was alive, our Sunday dinners were a real event. She’d make a pot roast, or maybe a baked ham with those scalloped potatoes she always got just right, and the whole house would smell like heaven. We’d sit down at the table, say grace, and really savor every single bite. We’d talk about the week, maybe the grandkids had called... that was enjoyment. That was real pleasure, taking your time and tasting your food. 

But this? What I do now in that kitchen? It’s the exact opposite of pleasure. There’s no savoring, doctor. Half the time, I’m not even really tasting what I’m putting in my mouth. It’s just... shoving it in. It’s like I’m a machine on an assembly line that’s gone completely haywire. I don't even bother to heat things up or put them on a plate most of the time. I’ll take a frozen waffle right out of the cardboard box and just start gnawing on it, or I'll eat cold baked beans straight out of the tin with a tablespoon. How could there be any pleasure in that? 

It's just this frantic, desperate feeling. My heart is pounding away in my chest, my mind is yelling at me to stop, and I’m just swallowing as fast as I possibly can. It’s not about enjoying the taste of a good meal, it’s just about... well, just obeying whatever broken wire in my head is telling me to keep going. If someone walked in and saw me, they wouldn't see a man enjoying a snack. They'd see a man who looks like he hasn't eaten in a month, just desperately tearing into whatever he can find. So no, if someone told me I was having a good time during all that, I’d tell them they were out of their mind. It’s pure misery from the very first bite to the last, just a terrible, mechanical compulsion that I wouldn't wish on my worst enemy.

I don't think I could ever look them in the eye again. I mean, a man my age should have some dignity. My father, he was a stoic man, worked at the mill for forty years, never complained, never lost his composure. What would he think if he saw his son acting like this? \n\nAnd the waste, doctor, the sheer waste of it all! I grew up when money was tight, you didn't waste food. Then... well, then comes the part where I have to get rid of it, which is a whole other layer of humiliation. If someone walked in and saw me, they wouldn't see a man enjoying a snack. They'd see a man who looks like he hasn't eaten in a month, just desperately tearing into whatever he can find. You start focusing more on just keeping your joints moving in the morning and hoping for a decent night's sleep without having to get up to use the washroom three times. So, no, I can't say I've had any issues in that department, mostly because there just isn't anything happening there to have an issue with! \n\nIt's honestly the furthest thing from my mind these days, especially with all this... this food business taking up every waking thought I seem to have. I mean, who could even think about intimacy or companionship in that way when you're spending your days wrestling with your own self in the kitchen, feeling so dirty and ashamed all the time? It just takes over everything. So no, no problems with a sex life, just... well, just the usual quiet that comes with being an old widower living alone in a big, empty house, I suppose.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel any pleasure or enjoyment during these eating episodes?\n\nPatient: Pleasure? Enjoyment? Good heavens, no. No, doctor, there is absolutely no joy in it whatsoever. You'd think there would be, wouldn't you? I mean, eating is supposed to be one of life's simple pleasures, especially at my age when you don't have too many vices left. \n\nI remember when Mary was alive, our Sunday dinners were a real event. She’d make a pot roast, or maybe a baked ham with those scalloped potatoes she always got just right, and the whole house would smell like heaven. We’d sit down at the table, say grace, and really savor every single bite. We’d talk about the week, maybe the grandkids had called... that was enjoyment. That was real pleasure, taking your time and tasting your food. \n\nBut this? What I do now in that kitchen? It’s the exact opposite of pleasure. There’s no savoring, doctor. Half the time, I’m not even really tasting what I’m putting in my mouth. It’s just... shoving it in. It’s like I’m a machine on an assembly line that’s gone completely haywire. I don't even bother to heat things up or put them on a plate most of the time. I’ll take a frozen waffle right out of the cardboard box and just start gnawing on it, or I'll eat cold baked beans straight out of the tin with a tablespoon. How could there be any pleasure in that? \n\nIt's just this frantic, desperate feeling. My heart is pounding away in my chest, my mind is yelling at me to stop, and I’m just swallowing as fast as I possibly can. It’s not about enjoying the taste of a good meal, it’s just about... well, just obeying whatever broken wire in my head is telling me to keep going. If someone walked in and saw me, they wouldn't see a man enjoying a snack. They'd see a man who looks like he hasn't eaten in a month, just desperately tearing into whatever he can find. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
How often? Well, it's... it's a lot, doctor. It's really quite a lot. I actually started keeping a little notebook, you know, a food log, because my daughter Sarah—she lives out in Seattle, lovely girl, always checking up on her old man—she suggested I write down what I eat just to keep track of my digestion. But, well, the notebook turned into something else entirely. 

If you look at those pages... and I have them right here in my coat pocket if you want to see... for months now, many, many months, it's been happening almost every single week. Nearly every week there's at least one afternoon, usually on a Tuesday or a Thursday when the house is just so dreadfully quiet and I've finished reading the morning paper. That's when it hits me. I'll just completely lose control. The log shows it all right there in black and white—the sheer amount of food, the frantic eating. 

And then, of course, the notebook also shows what comes after. Because I can't just leave it at that, can I? I have to... I try to make up for it. I'll write down how I forced myself to be sick, which is just awful, or how I took those laxatives I bought at the pharmacy down on Main Street—the young clerk there always looks at me so strangely when I buy them in bulk. Or I'll just decide I'm not going to eat a single thing for the next two days, just water and black tea, trying to punish myself, I suppose. 

Sometimes, if I don't do that, I'll try to work it off. I'll push myself to walk for hours around the neighborhood, way past what my knees can handle, just walking and walking until my joints are screaming at me. Or I'll do chores, heavy chores that I have no business doing at 78, like scrubbing the baseboards or cleaning out the gutters, just pushing and pushing myself to try and undo what I did in the kitchen. It's an exhausting cycle, doctor, and looking at this little notebook... it just breaks my heart to see how often it's happening. Week after week after week, the same terrible routine.

Vomit... well, yes. Yes, I do. It's... it's terribly shameful to say out loud to another human being, doctor, but yes. 

After I eat all that food, my stomach gets so painfully stretched out, it feels like it might just burst. And this terrible panic sets in. I go straight down the hall to the guest bathroom—I can't use the master bathroom for this, I just can't, because Mary's perfumes and her little decorative soaps are still in there, and I can't bear to do something so filthy in a place that reminds me of her. And I lean over that cold porcelain toilet, which is terribly hard on my lower back and my knees these days, let me tell you, and I... well, I make myself bring it all back up. I force myself to be sick. 

It's just miserable. My eyes water, my throat burns, my chest is heaving. But even then, even after going through all that wretched heaving... it's rarely enough to stop the panic. Because I start thinking about whatever might have slipped past, whatever might still be down there digesting. I get so incredibly scared that the food will stay in me. That fear just grips me tight, this absolute terror that it's going to stay inside my body and I won't be able to get it out. 

So that's when I turn to the laxatives. Like I mentioned before, I buy them down on Main Street, and I'll take them right then and there just to make absolutely sure everything is flushed out of my system. I take them entirely because I’m so scared the food will stay in me. It strips you of all your dignity, it really does, spending your twilight years huddled in a bathroom, relying on pills and making yourself sick just to empty yourself out. You'd think a man my age would know better, would have some grace, but when that fear takes hold, all my common sense just goes right out the window.

Well, doctor, I suppose it goes right back to what I was telling you earlier about that little notebook I keep in my pocket. I know I’m probably repeating myself—an old man's habit, I'm afraid, you'll have to forgive me—but it really is all written down right there in the ink. 

If you were to flip through those pages, my food logs show that for many months now... oh, goodness, it has to be at least half a year at this point... nearly every single week has had at least one afternoon where I just completely lost myself and ate out of control. And the vomiting goes hand-in-hand with that. So, to answer your question, the vomiting happens nearly every week, just like the eating. Whenever I have one of those spells, usually on those quiet Tuesdays or Thursdays I mentioned, I end up right back in that guest bathroom trying to undo it. 

Because I can never just let it be, you see. I always, always try to make up for what I’ve done. If I don't manage to bring it all up, or if the panic is still sitting heavy in my chest, that’s when I turn to the other things I was telling you about. The logs show it all, week after week—the vomiting, taking those awful laxatives, fasting for days on end with nothing but hot water and a tea bag, or just pushing myself to the absolute limit by walking for hours or doing heavy chores that my poor knees can barely handle anymore. 

It’s like a terrible ritual I can't escape. Every week, there's the eating, and then there's the desperate scramble to fix it, one way or another. I just... I get so tired, doctor. I really do. At seventy-eight, you'd think I'd be spending my afternoons reading or watching the birds out on the porch, not tallying up how many times I've made myself sick this month.

But just standing there in the aftermath, looking at the mess I made... it's just so deeply embarrassing. I'll spend the rest of the day just sitting in my recliner, staring at the television but not really watching it, just beating myself up over and over again. \"Why did you do that, Tom? Why couldn't you just walk away?\" It's a terrible, lonely feeling, doctor. Just sitting there stewing in your own regret.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any issues with your sex life recently?\n\nPatient: Sex life? Oh... well, no, doctor. No, not at all. I mean, you have to remember, I’m 78 years old. And with my Mary gone—like I mentioned before, my late wife—bless her heart, it’s been a good while now since she passed away. We had a wonderful marriage, we really did, fifty-two years we were together, through thick and thin, raised our kids, saw the grandkids come along. But... well, romance and all that sort of thing, it really hasn't been a part of my daily life for quite a long time now. \n\nEven before she got sick at the end, you know how it is, things just naturally slow down when you get to be an older fellow. You start focusing more on just keeping your joints moving in the morning and hoping for a decent night's sleep without having to get up to use the washroom three times. So, no, I can't say I've had any issues in that department, mostly because there just isn't anything happening there to have an issue with! \n\nIt's honestly the furthest thing from my mind these days, especially with all this... this food business taking up every waking thought I seem to have. I mean, who could even think about intimacy or companionship in that way when you're spending your days wrestling with your own self in the kitchen, feeling so dirty and ashamed all the time? It just takes over everything. So no, no problems with a sex life, just... well, just the usual quiet that comes with being an old widower living alone in a big, empty house, I suppose.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel any pleasure or enjoyment during these eating episodes?\n\nPatient: Pleasure? Enjoyment? Good heavens, no. No, doctor, there is absolutely no joy in it whatsoever. You'd think there would be, wouldn't you? I mean, eating is supposed to be one of life's simple pleasures, especially at my age when you don't have too many vices left. \n\nI remember when Mary was alive, our Sunday dinners were a real event. She’d make a pot roast, or maybe a baked ham with those scalloped potatoes she always got just right, and the whole house would smell like heaven. We’d sit down at the table, say grace, and really savor every single bite. We’d talk about the week, maybe the grandkids had called... that was enjoyment. That was real pleasure, taking your time and tasting your food. \n\nBut this? What I do now in that kitchen? It’s the exact opposite of pleasure. There’s no savoring, doctor. Half the time, I’m not even really tasting what I’m putting in my mouth. It’s just... shoving it in. It’s like I’m a machine on an assembly line that’s gone completely haywire. I don't even bother to heat things up or put them on a plate most of the time. I’ll take a frozen waffle right out of the cardboard box and just start gnawing on it, or I'll eat cold baked beans straight out of the tin with a tablespoon. How could there be any pleasure in that? \n\nIt's just this frantic, desperate feeling. My heart is pounding away in my chest, my mind is yelling at me to stop, and I’m just swallowing as fast as I possibly can. It’s not about enjoying the taste of a good meal, it’s just about... well, just obeying whatever broken wire in my head is telling me to keep going. If someone walked in and saw me, they wouldn't see a man enjoying a snack. They'd see a man who looks like he hasn't eaten in a month, just desperately tearing into whatever he can find. So no, if someone told me I was having a good time during all that, I’d tell them they were out of their mind. It’s pure misery from the very first bite to the last, just a terrible, mechanical compulsion that I wouldn't wish on my worst enemy.\n\nDoctor: How often do these eating episodes happen to you?\n\nPatient: How often? Well, it's... it's a lot, doctor. It's really quite a lot. I actually started keeping a little notebook, you know, a food log, because my daughter Sarah—she lives out in Seattle, lovely girl, always checking up on her old man—she suggested I write down what I eat just to keep track of my digestion. But, well, the notebook turned into something else entirely. \n\nIf you look at those pages... and I have them right here in my coat pocket if you want to see... for months now, many, many months, it's been happening almost every single week. Nearly every week there's at least one afternoon, usually on a Tuesday or a Thursday when the house is just so dreadfully quiet and I've finished reading the morning paper. That's when it hits me. I'll just completely lose control. The log shows it all right there in black and white—the sheer amount of food, the frantic eating. \n\nAnd then, of course, the notebook also shows what comes after. Because I can't just leave it at that, can I? I have to... I try to make up for it. I'll write down how I forced myself to be sick, which is just awful, or how I took those laxatives I bought at the pharmacy down on Main Street—the young clerk there always looks at me so strangely when I buy them in bulk. Or I'll just decide I'm not going to eat a single thing for the next two days, just water and black tea, trying to punish myself, I suppose. \n\nSometimes, if I don't do that, I'll try to work it off. I'll push myself to walk for hours around the neighborhood, way past what my knees can handle, just walking and walking until my joints are screaming at me. Or I'll do chores, heavy chores that I have no business doing at 78, like scrubbing the baseboards or cleaning out the gutters, just pushing and pushing myself to try and undo what I did in the kitchen. It's an exhausting cycle, doctor, and looking at this little notebook... it just breaks my heart to see how often it's happening. Week after week after week, the same terrible routine.\n\nDoctor: Do you usually make yourself vomit after one of these eating episodes?\n\nPatient: Vomit... well, yes. Yes, I do. It's... it's terribly shameful to say out loud to another human being, doctor, but yes. \n\nAfter I eat all that food, my stomach gets so painfully stretched out, it feels like it might just burst. And this terrible panic sets in. So I go to the guest bath, and I actually lock the door even though I live completely alone, if you can believe the absurdity of that. And I lean over that cold porcelain toilet, which is terribly hard on my lower back and my knees these days, let me tell you, and I... well, I make myself bring it all back up. I force myself to be sick. \n\nIt's just miserable. My eyes water, my throat burns, my chest is heaving. Because I start thinking about whatever might have slipped past, whatever might still be down there digesting. I get so incredibly scared that the food will stay in me. That fear just grips me tight, this absolute terror that it's going to stay inside my body and I won't be able to get it out. \n\nSo that's when I turn to the laxatives. Like I mentioned before, I buy them down on Main Street, and I'll take them right then and there just to make absolutely sure everything is flushed out of my system. I take them entirely because I’m so scared the food will stay in me. It strips you of all your dignity, it really does, spending your twilight years huddled in a bathroom, relying on pills and making yourself sick just to empty yourself out. You'd think a man my age would know better, would have some grace, but when that fear takes hold, all my common sense just goes right out the window.\n\nDoctor: How often do you make yourself vomit after one of these eating episodes?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, I suppose it goes right back to what I was telling you earlier about that little notebook I keep in my pocket. Changes in my weight? Well, it's funny you should ask that, doctor, because my weight is... well, it's something I keep a very, very close eye on. Probably too close of an eye, if I'm being perfectly honest with you. I have this old mechanical scale sitting right there in the master bathroom—the bathroom I told you I don't use for... for the other business, where Mary's things still are. I step on that scale every single morning, sometimes twice a day if I'm feeling particularly anxious about what I might have eaten. 

My regular physician, Dr. Evans down at the community clinic, he actually fusses at me about it quite a bit. He keeps looking at my charts and telling me I'm too thin, that a man my age needs a bit more meat on his bones to stay sturdy in case of a fall. He says I'm losing too much. 

But doctor, I just... I can't see it the way he does. I simply can't. Because even with my doctor sitting there looking me in the eye and saying I’m too thin, if I step on my scale at home and that little needle is up even just half a pound from the day before... just half a pound... this terrible, suffocating panic washes over me. 

It's the most dreadful feeling. I feel so incredibly ashamed. I look down at that number and I just think that I’ve completely let myself go, like I'm just a foolish, lazy old man who has no self-control whatsoever. It feels like a complete moral failure, if that makes any sense to you. And that panic, it just screams at me that I have to fix it right away. I have to undo it immediately, before it turns into a whole pound, or five pounds. I can't just let that half-pound sit there, I have to get it off right that very second, which is what drives me to do all those awful things I was just telling you about. So, to answer your question... maybe there haven't been significant changes upward, because I fight so desperately to prevent it, but the fear of gaining even a fraction of an ounce, well, it absolutely rules my entire life.

Well, yes, absolutely. I suppose I practically just answered that without meaning to, didn't I? But yes, it's exactly like I was just saying... it's all completely tied together. The fear is at the bottom of every single bit of it.

They see me out walking the dog, they wave, they think, \"There goes Tom, nice old fellow, got his life together.\" If they could see me in that kitchen... if they knew what I was doing, gorging myself like some kind of animal... I don't think I could ever look them in the eye again. I mean, a man my age should have some dignity. My father, he was a stoic man, worked at the mill for forty years, never complained, never lost his composure. What would he think if he saw his son acting like this? \n\nAnd the waste, doctor, the sheer waste of it all! I grew up when money was tight, you didn't waste food. You cleaned your plate because you were lucky to have it. And here I am, practically inhaling perfectly good food, not even tasting it, just shoving it in until I'm sick. Then... well, then comes the part where I have to get rid of it, which is a whole other layer of humiliation. But just standing there in the aftermath, looking at the mess I made... it's just so deeply embarrassing. I'll spend the rest of the day just sitting in my recliner, staring at the television but not really watching it, just beating myself up over and over again. \"Why did you do that, Tom? Why couldn't you just walk away?\" It's a terrible, lonely feeling, doctor. Just sitting there stewing in your own regret.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any issues with your sex life recently?\n\nPatient: Sex life? Oh... well, no, doctor. No, not at all. I mean, you have to remember, I’m 78 years old. And with my Mary gone—like I mentioned before, my late wife—bless her heart, it’s been a good while now since she passed away. We had a wonderful marriage, we really did, fifty-two years we were together, through thick and thin, raised our kids, saw the grandkids come along. But... well, romance and all that sort of thing, it really hasn't been a part of my daily life for quite a long time now. \n\nEven before she got sick at the end, you know how it is, things just naturally slow down when you get to be an older fellow. You start focusing more on just keeping your joints moving in the morning and hoping for a decent night's sleep without having to get up to use the washroom three times. You start focusing more on just keeping your joints moving in the morning and hoping for a decent night's sleep without having to get up to use the washroom three times. Oh, doctor... yes. Yes, absolutely. That is exactly it. Loss of control doesn't even begin to cover it, to be perfectly honest with you. It’s... well, it’s the most terrifying part of this whole miserable ordeal. 

You see, when I’m standing there in the kitchen—usually right there by the island where my Mary used to roll out her pie crusts, God rest her soul—and I start eating... it’s like my brain and my body just completely disconnect from one another. I don't know how else to explain it to someone who hasn't felt it. What scares me most is that once I start eating, it feels like my hands just keep reaching for more even while I’m telling myself, Tom, stop this right now. 

It’s like I’m a passenger in my own body, just helplessly watching some other fellow make a terrible, terrible mess of things. I'll be looking right at my own hand reaching back into the cookie jar, or pulling another and another slice of bread from the bag, and my mind is just screaming at me. I'll be standing there thinking, "Tom, you're a grown man, you're seventy-eight years old for heaven's sake, put that down, you know exactly how this is going to end, you know the panic that's coming." But my hands... they just don't listen to me. They just keep moving, bringing more and more food to my mouth, completely ignoring my own common sense. 

It’s a complete and utter hijacking of my own willpower. I’ve always prided myself on being a disciplined man, you know? I worked hard my whole life, always kept a neat yard, always paid my bills on time... but in those moments, with the food, I have absolutely zero say in the matter. The control is just entirely gone, completely vanished, and I can't stop the train once it leaves the station until every last crumb is gone and I'm just left standing there in the quiet, looking at the wrappers and realizing what I've done. So yes, the loss of control is absolute. It's truly frightening.

To be trapped inside yourself like that, unable to hit the brakes.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel guilty or ashamed after one of these eating episodes?\n\nPatient: Guilty? Ashamed? Oh, doctor... you have no idea. The guilt is... it's heavy. It's like a physical weight sitting right on my chest. As soon as it's over, as soon as the frenzy stops and I'm just standing there looking at the empty wrappers and the crumbs all over the counter... the shame just washes over me like a cold bucket of water. \n\nI think about my neighbors, you know? The Millers next door, or Mrs. Higgins across the street. They see me out walking the dog, they wave, they think, \"There goes Tom, nice old fellow, got his life together.\" If they could see me in that kitchen... if they knew what I was doing, gorging myself like some kind of animal... Or I'll just decide I'm not going to eat a single thing for the next two days, just water and black tea, trying to punish myself, I suppose. \n\nSometimes, if I don't do that, I'll try to work it off. I'll push myself to walk for hours around the neighborhood, way past what my knees can handle, just walking and walking until my joints are screaming at me. Or I'll do chores, heavy chores that I have no business doing at 78, like scrubbing the baseboards or cleaning out the gutters, just pushing and pushing myself to try and undo what I did in the kitchen. It's an exhausting cycle, doctor, and looking at this little notebook... it just breaks my heart to see how often it's happening. Week after week after week, the same terrible routine.\n\nDoctor: Do you usually make yourself vomit after one of these eating episodes?\n\nPatient: Vomit... well, yes. Yes, I do. It's... it's terribly shameful to say out loud to another human being, doctor, but yes. \n\nAfter I eat all that food, my stomach gets so painfully stretched out, it feels like it might just burst. And this terrible panic sets in. I go straight down the hall to the guest bathroom—I can't use the master bathroom for this, I just can't, because Mary's perfumes and her little decorative soaps are still in there, and I can't bear to do something so filthy in a place that reminds me of her. So I go to the guest bath, and I actually lock the door even though I live completely alone, if you can believe the absurdity of that. And I lean over that cold porcelain toilet, which is terribly hard on my lower back and my knees these days, let me tell you, and I... well, I make myself bring it all back up. I force myself to be sick. \n\nIt's just miserable. My eyes water, my throat burns, my chest is heaving. But even then, even after going through all that wretched heaving... it's rarely enough to stop the panic. Because I start thinking about whatever might have slipped past, whatever might still be down there digesting. I get so incredibly scared that the food will stay in me. That fear just grips me tight, this absolute terror that it's going to stay inside my body and I won't be able to get it out. \n\nSo that's when I turn to the laxatives. Like I mentioned before, I buy them down on Main Street, and I'll take them right then and there just to make absolutely sure everything is flushed out of my system. I take them entirely because I’m so scared the food will stay in me. It strips you of all your dignity, it really does, spending your twilight years huddled in a bathroom, relying on pills and making yourself sick just to empty yourself out. You'd think a man my age would know better, would have some grace, but when that fear takes hold, all my common sense just goes right out the window.\n\nDoctor: How often do you make yourself vomit after one of these eating episodes?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, I suppose it goes right back to what I was telling you earlier about that little notebook I keep in my pocket. I know I’m probably repeating myself—an old man's habit, I'm afraid, you'll have to forgive me—but it really is all written down right there in the ink. \n\nIf you were to flip through those pages, my food logs show that for many months now... oh, goodness, it has to be at least half a year at this point... nearly every single week has had at least one afternoon where I just completely lost myself and ate out of control. And the vomiting goes hand-in-hand with that. So, to answer your question, the vomiting happens nearly every week, just like the eating. Whenever I have one of those spells, usually on those quiet Tuesdays or Thursdays I mentioned, I end up right back in that guest bathroom trying to undo it. \n\nBecause I can never just let it be, you see. I always, always try to make up for what I’ve done. If I don't manage to bring it all up, or if the panic is still sitting heavy in my chest, that’s when I turn to the other things I was telling you about. The logs show it all, week after week—the vomiting, taking those awful laxatives, fasting for days on end with nothing but hot water and a tea bag, or just pushing myself to the absolute limit by walking for hours or doing heavy chores that my poor knees can barely handle anymore. \n\nIt’s like a terrible ritual I can't escape. Every week, there's the eating, and then there's the desperate scramble to fix it, one way or another. I just... I get so tired, doctor. I really do. At seventy-eight, you'd think I'd be spending my afternoons reading or watching the birds out on the porch, not tallying up how many times I've made myself sick this month.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over the past few months?\n\nPatient: Changes in my weight? Well, it's funny you should ask that, doctor, because my weight is... well, it's something I keep a very, very close eye on. Probably too close of an eye, if I'm being perfectly honest with you. I have this old mechanical scale sitting right there in the master bathroom—the bathroom I told you I don't use for... for the other business, where Mary's things still are. I step on that scale every single morning, sometimes twice a day if I'm feeling particularly anxious about what I might have eaten. \n\nMy regular physician, Dr. Evans down at the community clinic, he actually fusses at me about it quite a bit. He keeps looking at my charts and telling me I'm too thin, that a man my age needs a bit more meat on his bones to stay sturdy in case of a fall. He says I'm losing too much. \n\nBut doctor, I just... I can't see it the way he does. I simply can't. Because even with my doctor sitting there looking me in the eye and saying I’m too thin, if I step on my scale at home and that little needle is up even just half a pound from the day before... just half a pound... this terrible, suffocating panic washes over me. \n\nIt's the most dreadful feeling. I feel so incredibly ashamed. I look down at that number and I just think that I’ve completely let myself go, like I'm just a foolish, lazy old man who has no self-control whatsoever. It feels like a complete moral failure, if that makes any sense to you. And that panic, it just screams at me that I have to fix it right away. I have to undo it immediately, before it turns into a whole pound, or five pounds. I can't just let that half-pound sit there, I have to get it off right that very second, which is what drives me to do all those awful things I was just telling you about. So, to answer your question... maybe there haven't been significant changes upward, because I fight so desperately to prevent it, but the fear of gaining even a fraction of an ounce, well, it absolutely rules my entire life.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your eating episodes and subsequent behaviors are related to a fear of gaining weight?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, absolutely. I suppose I practically just answered that without meaning to, didn't I? But yes, it's exactly like I was just saying... it's all completely tied together. The fear is at the bottom of every single bit of it. \n\nYou know, even with Dr. Evans sitting there with his medical degree telling me I'm too thin, warning me about my bones and my balance... none of his wisdom makes a lick of difference when I'm alone in that house. If I step on that scale and see it up by just half a pound, I get so panicky and ashamed. It’s like a physical weight sitting right on my chest. I just think I’ve completely let myself go, that I'm becoming this... this lazy, heavy old man who can't even control his own appetite. \n\nAnd that's exactly why I do all those awful things afterwards. I just have to fix it right away. The fear of that half-pound staying on my body, it just drives me right into the guest bathroom to make myself sick, or sends me walking for hours on these bad knees. And the tragic part of it all, doctor, is that sometimes I'm so worried about my weight all day long, so stressed about what I'm allowed to eat and what I'm not, that the pressure just builds and builds until I finally break down and have one of those eating episodes in the first place! It’s a vicious, vicious circle. I worry about the weight, I get overwhelmed and eat, and then the fear comes roaring back so fiercely that I'm scrambling to undo it. \n\nSo yes, it is all because I am absolutely terrified of putting on weight. If I wasn't so scared of the scale going up, I wouldn't be spending my retirement years locked in a bathroom trying to empty out my own stomach. It really does dictate every single day of my life.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever experience a period of time where you eat a large amount of food in a short time, and then try to compensate for it by purging or using laxatives, and does this cycle happen regularly?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, I know we’ve been circling around this very thing, haven't we? I feel like a broken record today, but yes, that cycle... that's exactly what my life has become. It’s exactly as I was saying about those quiet afternoons. You see, since my Mary passed, the house just gets so terribly silent. Sometimes the only thing I can hear is the hum of the refrigerator or the ticking of the old grandfather clock in the hallway, and the emptiness just sort of... well, it swallows me up. \n\nAnd when one of those spells hits me on those afternoons alone at the house... it's almost like I'm in a trance. I don't even realize what I'm doing until the damage is already done. I can go through an entire loaf of bread, just pulling out slice after slice, and then I'll get into the peanut butter, digging it right out of the jar with a spoon. And it doesn't stop there, no... I'll find a whole package of cookies, whatever cold leftovers are sitting in the Tupperware from the night before, and then finish it off with a carton of ice cream. I eat all of it, just desperately eating and eating in one sitting before I even really look up and see the wrappers and the empty plates scattered all over the kitchen counter. \n\nIt’s shameful, doctor. It really, truly is. I look at the mess and I can't believe what I've done. And then, of course, that terrible panic I was telling you about just grips me by the throat. The guilt is unbearable. So yes, that's exactly when I rush to the guest bathroom to make myself sick, or I reach for those awful laxatives, because I just can't let all that food sit inside me and turn into weight. And this whole dreadful routine... yes, it happens regularly. Week after week, just like I wrote down in my little notebook. I wish I could tell you it was just a rare mistake, just an old man's momentary lapse in judgment, but it's a constant, exhausting cycle that just won't let me go.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever feel a loss of control during these eating episodes where you're consuming a large amount of food?\n\nPatient: Oh, doctor... yes. Yes, absolutely. That is exactly it. Loss of control doesn't even begin to cover it, to be perfectly honest with you. It’s... well, it’s the most terrifying part of this whole miserable ordeal. \n\nYou see, when I’m standing there in the kitchen—usually right there by the island where my Mary used to roll out her pie crusts, God rest her soul—and I start eating... it’s like my brain and my body just completely disconnect from one another. I don't know how else to explain it to someone who hasn't felt it. What scares me most is that once I start eating, it feels like my hands just keep reaching for more even while I’m telling myself, Tom, stop this right now. \n\nIt’s like I’m a passenger in my own body, just helplessly watching some other fellow make a terrible, terrible mess of things. I'll be looking right at my own hand reaching back into the cookie jar, or pulling another and another slice of bread from the bag, and my mind is just screaming at me. I'll be standing there thinking, \"Tom, you're a grown man, you're seventy-eight years old for heaven's sake, put that down, you know exactly how this is going to end, you know the panic that's coming.\" But my hands... they just don't listen to me. They just keep moving, bringing more and more food to my mouth, completely ignoring my own common sense. \n\nIt’s a complete and utter hijacking of my own willpower. I’ve always prided myself on being a disciplined man, you know? I worked hard my whole life, always kept a neat yard, always paid my bills on time... but in those moments, with the food, I have absolutely zero say in the matter. The control is just entirely gone, completely vanished, and I can't stop the train once it leaves the station until every last crumb is gone and I'm just left standing there in the quiet, looking at the wrappers and realizing what I've done. Well, I... I actually brought my little notebook with me today, the one I mentioned to you earlier. I started keeping track, you see, writing down what I eat and what happens afterward. Other thoughts... well, yes. Yes, there is something else that just... it just eats away at me, day in and day out. It’s this constant, exhausting worry that I just can't seem to turn off, no matter how hard I try. 

You see, I go to my regular physician—Dr. Miller, over at the family practice clinic—and he's been telling me lately, "Tom, you're too thin. You're losing too much." He looks at my chart, looks at me over his little reading glasses, and tells me I need to put some meat on my bones. But doctor, I hear the words he's saying, but my mind just absolutely refuses to believe him. Because... well, I have this old scale in the master bathroom. Mary bought it at Sears years and years ago, the heavy kind with the little dial that spins around. And I step on it every single morning, first thing, before I've even had a drop of tap water or put my slippers on. 

And I tell you, even with my doctor saying I’m too thin, if I look down between my toes and see that the scale is up even half a pound... just half a pound, mind you... I feel so incredibly panicky. My heart just drops right into my stomach and starts racing. I feel this deep, terrible shame, just washing all over me, like I’ve completely let myself go. I look in the mirror and I just feel disgusted, thinking I'm turning into this lazy, heavy old man who has no discipline.

Well, no, doctor, not every single time. I'll push myself to walk for hours around the neighborhood, way past what my knees can handle, just walking and walking until my joints are screaming at me. It's an exhausting cycle, doctor, and looking at this little notebook... it just breaks my heart to see how often it's happening. It strips you of all your dignity, it really does, spending your twilight years huddled in a bathroom, relying on pills and making yourself sick just to empty yourself out. You'd think a man my age would know better, would have some grace, but when that fear takes hold, all my common sense just goes right out the window.\n\nDoctor: How often do you make yourself vomit after one of these eating episodes?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, I suppose it goes right back to what I was telling you earlier about that little notebook I keep in my pocket. I know I’m probably repeating myself—an old man's habit, I'm afraid, you'll have to forgive me—but it really is all written down right there in the ink. \n\nIf you were to flip through those pages, my food logs show that for many months now... oh, goodness, it has to be at least half a year at this point... nearly every single week has had at least one afternoon where I just completely lost myself and ate out of control. If I don't manage to bring it all up, or if the panic is still sitting heavy in my chest, that’s when I turn to the other things I was telling you about. The logs show it all, week after week—the vomiting, taking those awful laxatives, fasting for days on end with nothing but hot water and a tea bag, or just pushing myself to the absolute limit by walking for hours or doing heavy chores that my poor knees can barely handle anymore. \n\nIt’s like a terrible ritual I can't escape. Every week, there's the eating, and then there's the desperate scramble to fix it, one way or another. I just... I get so tired, doctor. I really do. At seventy-eight, you'd think I'd be spending my afternoons reading or watching the birds out on the porch, not tallying up how many times I've made myself sick this month.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over the past few months?\n\nPatient: Changes in my weight? Well, it's funny you should ask that, doctor, because my weight is... well, it's something I keep a very, very close eye on. Probably too close of an eye, if I'm being perfectly honest with you. I have this old mechanical scale sitting right there in the master bathroom—the bathroom I told you I don't use for... for the other business, where Mary's things still are. I step on that scale every single morning, sometimes twice a day if I'm feeling particularly anxious about what I might have eaten. \n\nMy regular physician, Dr. Evans down at the community clinic, he actually fusses at me about it quite a bit. Because even with my doctor sitting there looking me in the eye and saying I’m too thin, if I step on my scale at home and that little needle is up even just half a pound from the day before... just half a pound... this terrible, suffocating panic washes over me. \n\nIt's the most dreadful feeling. I feel so incredibly ashamed. I look down at that number and I just think that I’ve completely let myself go, like I'm just a foolish, lazy old man who has no self-control whatsoever. It feels like a complete moral failure, if that makes any sense to you. And that panic, it just screams at me that I have to fix it right away. I have to undo it immediately, before it turns into a whole pound, or five pounds. I can't just let that half-pound sit there, I have to get it off right that very second, which is what drives me to do all those awful things I was just telling you about. So, to answer your question... maybe there haven't been significant changes upward, because I fight so desperately to prevent it, but the fear of gaining even a fraction of an ounce, well, it absolutely rules my entire life.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your eating episodes and subsequent behaviors are related to a fear of gaining weight?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, absolutely. I suppose I practically just answered that without meaning to, didn't I? But yes, it's exactly like I was just saying... it's all completely tied together. The fear is at the bottom of every single bit of it. \n\nYou know, even with Dr. Evans sitting there with his medical degree telling me I'm too thin, warning me about my bones and my balance... none of his wisdom makes a lick of difference when I'm alone in that house. If I step on that scale and see it up by just half a pound, I get so panicky and ashamed. It’s like a physical weight sitting right on my chest. I just think I’ve completely let myself go, that I'm becoming this... this lazy, heavy old man who can't even control his own appetite. \n\nAnd that's exactly why I do all those awful things afterwards. I just have to fix it right away. The fear of that half-pound staying on my body, it just drives me right into the guest bathroom to make myself sick, or sends me walking for hours on these bad knees. And the tragic part of it all, doctor, is that sometimes I'm so worried about my weight all day long, so stressed about what I'm allowed to eat and what I'm not, that the pressure just builds and builds until I finally break down and have one of those eating episodes in the first place! It’s a vicious, vicious circle. I worry about the weight, I get overwhelmed and eat, and then the fear comes roaring back so fiercely that I'm scrambling to undo it. \n\nSo yes, it is all because I am absolutely terrified of putting on weight. If I wasn't so scared of the scale going up, I wouldn't be spending my retirement years locked in a bathroom trying to empty out my own stomach. It really does dictate every single day of my life.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever experience a period of time where you eat a large amount of food in a short time, and then try to compensate for it by purging or using laxatives, and does this cycle happen regularly?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, I know we’ve been circling around this very thing, haven't we? I feel like a broken record today, but yes, that cycle... that's exactly what my life has become. It’s exactly as I was saying about those quiet afternoons. You see, since my Mary passed, the house just gets so terribly silent. Sometimes the only thing I can hear is the hum of the refrigerator or the ticking of the old grandfather clock in the hallway, and the emptiness just sort of... well, it swallows me up. \n\nAnd when one of those spells hits me on those afternoons alone at the house... it's almost like I'm in a trance. I eat all of it, just desperately eating and eating in one sitting before I even really look up and see the wrappers and the empty plates scattered all over the kitchen counter. \n\nIt’s shameful, doctor. I'll be standing there thinking, \"Tom, you're a grown man, you're seventy-eight years old for heaven's sake, put that down, you know exactly how this is going to end, you know the panic that's coming.\" But my hands... they just don't listen to me. They just keep moving, bringing more and more food to my mouth, completely ignoring my own common sense. \n\nIt’s a complete and utter hijacking of my own willpower. I’ve always prided myself on being a disciplined man, you know?
